findings.mechanism: Cost-to-edge gate: a market maker earns the spread, a retail grid pays it
findings.description: Every institutional grid- or market-making result we found makes its money by being paid the spread (or a maker rebate), not by holding inventory for a short time. Mende & Menkhoff studied a bank's EUR/USD book. Its profits were fully explained by spread revenue from intermediation. Its speculative positions did not become profitable within a 30-minute horizon. The hftbacktest high-frequency grid examples only make money because they assume the top Binance maker rebate (-0.005%). Chen et al. prove a plain grid has zero expected value. The user's MT5 grid sits on the other side: every layer and every TP or time-stop exit crosses the spread. Mechanism for the EA: before each session, and live on every L1 attempt, compute the expected gross reversal edge per layer for the current session and volatility. Compare it with the round-trip cost (spread + commission + slippage). Trade only when edge/cost is above about 1.5-2.
findings.blowup_protection: This is mainly about not bleeding to death rather than tail ruin. A strategy with negative net expectancy is certain to be ruined however well its risk is managed. This gate stops the EA from running in sessions or on brokers where expected value per basket is below zero. It also enforces a spread guard tied to TP size, not a fixed number of points.
findings.hf_relevance: Critical at 1-30 minutes because TPs are only a few pips, so a 1.0-1.4 pip round-trip cost is 20-40% of each win. Our own M1 stats (inference) put the average reversal after a 1-3 sigma move at only about +0.2 to +0.5 pips over the next 5-30 minutes, which is below standard-account costs. Only raw-spread ECN pricing, or a cent account with tight spreads, can make the arithmetic work, and only in the best sessions.

The GLFT-simplified notebook (fetched) says profitability depends on rebates, not alpha. DGT paper (fetched README): a traditional grid is a 'zero-expectation system'. Own analysis (inference) of Oanda EURUSD M1 mid 2012-2020.05, sign-adjusted next-h reversal after a past-h move: 1-2 sigma moves +0.15..+0.43 pips; 2-3 sigma moves +0.04..+0.51 pips, by session and horizon (5/15/30 min). Breakeven basket win rate p_be = (L + c)/(W + L), where W = TP profit, L = loss at hard stop, c = total basket cost (inference). findings.mechanism: Hard inventory cap Q with one-sided quoting at the bound (GLFT / Avellaneda-Stoikov inventory limits)
findings.description: In the Gueant-Lehalle-Fernandez-Tapia solution the market maker solves the problem under an explicit inventory limit Q. At q = +Q or -Q the quotes are set so no more inventory can build up: the risk-increasing side simply stops quoting. hftbacktest's high-frequency grid does the same with a max_position of +/-5: buy orders are generated only if position < max_position, sell orders only if position > -max_position. Mechanism for the EA: MaxLayers becomes a hard cap of about 2-4 layers per side. Add a MaxNetLots cap on |buyLots - sellLots|. Once a side reaches its cap it never adds again in that cycle. That basket can then only exit by TP, by the decaying time-exit, or by the hard basket stop.
findings.blowup_protection: The worst-case loss becomes a known number computed before the trade: sum(lot_i x distance_i to stop). Without the cap a grid with no per-position stop has unbounded exposure. On a $100 standard account (inference), 3 flat 0.01 layers at 5-pip spacing with the stop one spacing past the last layer lose $3 (3%). The user's 18-layer v6.12 ladder was 7.81 lots per side, about $78 per pip.
findings.hf_relevance: Directly applicable. FX dealers' inventory half-life is minutes (Lyons: about 10 min), and they square up quickly (Bjonnes & Rime). A 1-30 minute grid should behave the same way: small, quickly recycled inventory, never a deep ladder.
findings.evidence: GLFT (search summary): the HJB reduces to linear ODEs under inventory constraints; 'at the boundaries q = Q or q = -Q, the quotes are set to avoid further inventory accumulation'; the approximations are 'used in practice by major banks'. hftbacktest HF grid (fetched): max_position 5, 20 levels, grid interval 10 ticks. Lyons 1995 (search summary): the dealer's position half-life was only 10 minutes. Bjonnes & Rime (search summary): dealers control inventory intensively and end the day near zero.
findings.parameter_hints: Pick Q from the risk budget, not from 'room to average': Q_lots such that loss_at_stop(Q) <= 1-2% of equity (standard $100: usually 2-3 x 0.01 flat; cent account: 0.10-0.30 cent-lots per layer). MaxNetLots <= Q. Count both grids: q_net = buyLots - sellLots.

findings.mechanism: Inventory-skewed TP and spacing (Avellaneda-Stoikov reservation price, GLFT skew), applied to net inventory across both grids
findings.description: Avellaneda-Stoikov shift the dealer's fair price against inventory: r = s - q*gamma*sigma^2*(T-t). Spread = gamma*sigma^2*(T-t) + (2/gamma)ln(1+gamma/k). GLFT's closed form gives bid depth = c1 + (Delta/2)*sigma*c2 + q*sigma*c2 and ask depth = c1 + (Delta/2)*sigma*c2 - q*sigma*c2. When long, the dealer sells more readily and buys less readily. Mechanism for the EA: treat q = buyLots - sellLots as the dealer's inventory. Make the overloaded side's TP closer: TP_side = TP0*(1 - k_tp*|q|/Q), floored at cost + 0.5 pip. Make its next-layer spacing wider: s_next = s0*(1 + k_s*|q|/Q). Leave the light side normal, so it keeps harvesting and naturally offsets q.
findings.blowup_protection: Inventory skew mostly cuts P&L variance and inventory dispersion for a small loss of mean. That is exactly the trade a small account needs. The cut in inventory variance lowers the chance of being at max inventory when a trend starts.
findings.hf_relevance: The EA's two independent grids already work like two-sided quotes. Adding the skew turns them into a crude AS market maker. The skew term scales with sigma^2*(T-t), so with a 30-minute horizon it should shrink as the basket nears its time limit and grow with session volatility.
findings.evidence: AS replication (iqueipopg, fetched), gamma=0.1: inventory strategy profit 65.0, std 6.6, vs symmetric 67.9, std 13.5. CloudWingsBD (fetched): final-q std 2.93 vs 8.40 at gamma=0.1 and 1.64 vs 5.17 at gamma=1.0; skewing keeps 70-100% of mean profit and cuts P&L std to 45-65%. Seb-L-P (fetched): Sharpe-like 9.93 vs 5.07, mean |inventory| 0.98 vs 4.37, Sharpe peaked at an interior gamma of about 0.1. GLFT-simplified notebook (fetched): bid_depth = half_spread*(1 + skew*normalized_position), ask_depth = half_spread*(1 - skew*normalized_position).
findings.parameter_hints: k_tp 0.3-0.5, k_s 0.3-0.6. Normalise q by Q. Choose k on an interior-optimum plateau, not at the edge of the search range (the Sharpe-vs-gamma curve has an interior peak). Recompute after every fill. Hedged-account margin uses the larger leg, but P&L risk is the net q.

findings.mechanism: Volatility-scaled spacing, TP and lot size (half-spread proportional to sigma; volatility targeting)
findings.description: In AS/GLFT the optimal half-spread and skew scale with sigma (and sigma^2). hftbacktest's practical simplification sets half_spread_tick = volatility*vol_to_half_spread, using a rolling 10-minute volatility, and snaps the grid interval to it. The Taranto-based MQL5 grid EA also uses ATR-dynamic spacing. Volatility targeting (Harvey et al.) cuts notional when volatility is high and reduces left-tail events across 60 assets. Mechanism for the EA: replace the fixed 7.5-pip spacing and 5.3-pip TP with multiples of a blended sigma_15. Blend the realised 15-minute sigma from the last 60-120 M1 bars with a same-hour seasonal prior. Set lot so that the pip-risk per basket in money is constant.
findings.blowup_protection: With fixed spacing, a high-volatility hour fills the whole ladder within minutes. Own stats (inference): 15-minute sigma ranges from 3.4 pips (04 UTC) to 8.8 pips (14 UTC), so a fixed 7.5 pips is about 2 sigma in Asia but under 1 sigma in the London/NY overlap. Sigma-scaling keeps ladder depth in sigma units constant. Inverse-sigma lot sizing keeps money at risk constant, which is what volatility targeting does for tails.
findings.hf_relevance: Essential at M1/M5 because intraday volatility has a strong U/W-shaped seasonality (Ito & Hashimoto; Andersen & Bollerslev). sigma_1m in our data: 1.0-1.3 pips in Asia, 2.0-2.4 pips in London and the overlap.
findings.evidence: hftbacktest (fetched): 'half_spread_tick = volatility * vol_to_half_spread', with volatility = nanstd(mid changes over a 10-min window)*sqrt(10). Harvey et al. (search summary): volatility targeting 'reduces tail risks across asset classes', because left-tail events happen when volatility is high and exposure is then small. Own stats (inference, /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-web/1e3fd826-2afd-5f35-81b2-b0221830643e/scratchpad/hfstats/hfstats.py): per-UTC-hour sd15 = 3.38-8.83 pips, sd1m = 0.98-2.37 pips.
findings.parameter_hints: spacing = 1.0 x sigma_15 (floor = 4 x cost), TP = 0.5-0.7 x sigma_15 from the weighted average, hard stop at 3 x sigma_15 from L1. lot = floor(RiskMoney / (pipValuePerLot x sum of layer distances to stop)) to the broker lot step. Use EWMA sigma with a 60-minute half-life, clipped to 0.7-1.5 x the hour-of-day median.

findings.mechanism: Depth limited to the reversion zone; cut at the persistence boundary (weak trends revert, significant trends persist)
findings.description: Schmidhuber & Safari cover minutes to decades across asset classes, including intraday tick data from 2 minutes to 1 day. On short scales markets are in a 'reversion regime', but in that regime only weak trends revert; trends that become statistically significant persist. Jurek & Yang derive the optimal arbitrage allocation for an OU mispricing. There is a critical mispricing beyond which further divergence should reduce the position: the 'stabilization region' is bounded, and outside it wealth effects dominate. Leung & Li show the optimal entry region is a bounded interval strictly above the stop level: you do not enter near the stop. Mechanism for the EA: all layers sit inside about +/-2 sigma_15 of L1. The hard basket stop sits at about 3 sigma_15. No layer is added within 1 spacing of the stop. When price leaves the ladder, close and re-centre later (dynamic grid reset) instead of extending it.
findings.blowup_protection: This turns 'average down forever' into a bounded bet that is only placed where the data says reversion exists. The 2014-15-style trend that killed the user's configs is by definition a 'statistically significant' move. The stop exits before the ladder gets deep, so the loss is capped at roughly the risk budget.
findings.hf_relevance: Our own EURUSD M1 data (inference) shows the same thing at 15-30 minutes. Sign-adjusted reversal is positive for 1-3 sigma moves (+0.2..+0.5 pips). It turns negative (continuation) for moves above 3 sigma in London AM (-0.76 pips at 15m), NY PM (-0.45 at 15m, -1.06 at 30m), the overlap (-2.01 at 30m) and rollover (-0.39/-0.90). Asia is the exception: >3 sigma moves still revert at 5-15m.
findings.evidence: Schmidhuber & Safari (search summary): 'In the reversion regime, weak trends tend to revert, while those trends that become statistically significant tend to persist.' Next return modelled as a positive linear term minus a negative cubic term in trend strength. Jurek-Yang (fetched arbitragelab doc): 'there is a critical level of the mispricing beyond which further divergence in the mispricing precipitates a reduction in the allocation'. Leung-Li (search summary): 'entry region is characterized by a bounded price interval that lies strictly above the stop-loss level'. DGT (fetched): resets the grid when price breaks the threshold.
findings.parameter_hints: Ladder span (L1 to last layer) <= 2 sigma_15. Hard basket stop at 2.5-3.5 sigma_15 from L1, broker-side SL on every ticket. MaxLayers = floor(2 sigma_15/spacing) + 1, typically 3. Session-dependent: allow up to 3.5 sigma in Asia, 2.5-3 sigma in London/NY.

findings.mechanism: Linear (flat) inventory per level, scaled by wealth; no convex lot ladder
findings.description: For log utility and an OU mispricing, Jurek & Yang's optimal allocation is N = kappa*(Sbar - S)/sigma^2 * W. That is linear in the deviation and proportional to current wealth W. Flat lots per grid level give exactly linear inventory in the deviation. A +LotIncrement ladder (0.01, 0.02, 0.03...) gives inventory quadratic in the deviation, and a doubling ladder exponential. Both over-allocate at depth, exactly where Jurek-Yang say allocation should start falling and where Schmidhuber-Safari find persistence. A 2026 grid paper tried 'soft martingale' sub-linear multipliers and still had 80% equity drawdown. Mechanism for the EA: FlatLayers = MaxLayers (no increment), or at most one extra unit on the last layer. Base lot is a function of equity and sigma, not a constant.
findings.blowup_protection: Convex ladders make loss grow faster than the distance moved: with +0.01/layer, 6 layers at 7.5 pips lose $42 (42% of $100) at the stop, vs $15.75 for flat 0.01 (inference). Linear inventory times a wealth factor shrinks positions after losses, the anti-martingale property that prevents ruin.
findings.hf_relevance: The user wants 'start 0.01 and scale up per layer'. The literature says scale with equity and with sigma (between baskets), not with adverse distance (within a basket). On a $100 standard account the 0.01 minimum lot already makes 3 flat layers about 2-3% risk, so there is no room to scale up per layer at all. A cent account is needed for granularity.
findings.evidence: Jurek-Yang (fetched): N(W,S,tau) = ((kappa(Sbar - S) - rS)/sigma^2) W for gamma=1. MDPI ML-augmented HF grid (search summary): soft martingale linspace(1,5,10) cut 4-level exposure by 63% vs 2x doubling. Out-of-sample on EUR/USD H1: 65.77% win rate, PF 2.85, yet maximum equity drawdown 79.97% vs balance drawdown 13.98% (DDR 5.72). Own ladder table (inference): s=5, L=5 flat=$7.50 vs +0.01/layer=$17.50; s=10, L=6 flat=$21 vs +0.01/layer=$56 on $100.
findings.parameter_hints: LotIncrement = 0, FlatLayers = MaxLayers. BaseLot = clamp(floor_to_step(f x Equity / (pipValuePerLot x sum of distances to stop)), minLot, maxLot), with f = risk fraction (see the Kelly finding). Recompute only when a new cycle starts.

findings.mechanism: Terminal-time liquidation: separate entry and exit deadlines, time-decaying TP, hard 30-minute close
findings.description: Market-making models have a horizon T. In AS the skew/spread term gamma*sigma^2*(T-t) shrinks as t -> T and inventory is valued and liquidated at T. Cartea-Jaimungal add a terminal liquidation penalty plus a running inventory penalty; the running penalty is the more effective control. Kitapbayev & Leung solve mean-reversion trading with one deadline to enter and a later one to exit. Both boundaries are time-varying and the trading region changes significantly near the deadline. Lipton & Lopez de Prado optimise profit-take and stop-loss jointly with a maximum trade duration T. Mechanism for the EA: a basket clock starts at L1. No new layers after T_add. From T_decay the TP target falls linearly toward break-even plus cost. At T_max = 30 minutes everything is closed at market, and every basket is flattened before session end.
findings.blowup_protection: This caps how long inventory can sit through a developing trend. It also stops a basket from turning into the multi-day, swap-paying positions that drove the user's losses (swap was the largest cost in their study). Note that a time stop does not cap price loss on its own: inside 30 minutes our data shows 99th/99.9th percentile one-sided moves of 31-35 / 55-60 pips in London/NY. It must be paired with the hard price stop.
findings.hf_relevance: This is the core of the user's 1-30 minute requirement. Dealers' inventory half-life of about 10 minutes (Lyons) means a 30-minute limit is about 3 half-lives. Liquidating by market order costs the spread (the CJ terminal penalty), so a TP that decays toward break-even + cost exits more cheaply than a hard stop.
findings.evidence: CJR (search summary): 'the running penalty is much more effective than the terminal inventory constraint'; terminal inventory liquidated with a penalty of 1-10 bps. Kitapbayev-Leung (search summary): 'optimal trading boundaries are time-varying and the trading region changes significantly near the trading deadline'. Lipton-LdP doc (fetched): SR maximised over profit-take >= 0 and stop-loss <= 0 subject to max duration T; example scaled result: profit 5.075, stop -3.410, max duration 1.96. Own stats (inference): one-sided 30-min MAE p50/p99/p99.9 = 2.2/17.5/36.4 pips (Asia), 4.7/34.9/59.9 (overlap), 9.4/99.6/148.3 in news windows.
findings.parameter_hints: T_add = 15-20 min (no layers after it), T_decay = 10 min, T_max = 30 min (hard). TP(t) = max(cost + 0.3 pip, TP0 x (1 - (t - T_decay)/(T_max - T_decay))). Last L1 entry = session_end - T_max. Optionally add a running penalty: shrink TP faster when q is large.

findings.mechanism: OU-calibrated optimal bands and a mean-reversion-speed filter (Bertram; Leung-Li; Lipton-Lopez de Prado; Avellaneda-Lee)
findings.description: Bertram gives analytic expected trade length and return per unit time for OU entry/exit bands. Return per trade is (m - a - c) and return per unit time is r/E[T]. With costs, the optimal bands are symmetric around the mean. Leung-Li add costs and a stop: a tighter (higher) stop always lowers the optimal take-profit, and entry becomes a bounded interval. Avellaneda & Lee's stat-arb desk only trades residuals whose estimated mean-reversion speed kappa is fast relative to the estimation window. Mechanism for the EA, run each M5 bar: (1) fit an AR(1)/OU to M1 deviations from a 60-120 minute EMA, giving kappa, sigma and half-life; (2) trade only if half-life <= 8-10 minutes (so T_max covers at least 3 half-lives) and the OU stationary sd >= 4 x cost; (3) set spacing, TP and stop from the Bertram / Lipton-LdP optimum for that (kappa, sigma, c), maximising Sharpe per unit time rather than raw profit.
findings.blowup_protection: It refuses to arm a grid when the market is not mean-reverting on the grid's own timescale (slow kappa = trend). Those are the regimes where averaging-down accumulates losing inventory.
findings.hf_relevance: OU tools are built for exactly this horizon when calibrated on M1 data. Our variance ratios (inference) show 30-minute mean reversion varying by hour. VR30 is about 0.54-0.67 at 20-21 UTC, 0.74 at 03-04 UTC and 0.76-0.78 at 15-16 UTC, but about 1.02-1.04 (no reversion) at 05-07 UTC and 1.05 in news windows. So the filter will switch on and off within the day.
findings.evidence: Bertram doc (fetched): E[T] = (pi/mu)(Erfi((m-theta)sqrt(mu)/sigma) - Erfi((a-theta)sqrt(mu)/sigma)); mu_s = (m - a - c)/E[T]; optimum at (m-theta)^2 = (a-theta)^2. Example with c=0.001 gives a = -0.004, m = 0.004. Leung-Li (search summary): 'a higher stop-loss level always implies a lower optimal take-profit level'. Avellaneda-Lee (search summary): only stocks with fast mean reversion (kappa*T >= 1) are traded. Wisniewska (search summary): mean reversion present in 1-minute EURUSD (ADF rejects a unit root around the moving mean).
findings.parameter_hints: Half-life = ln2/kappa from an AR(1) on 1-minute deviations: trade if HL <= 10 min and stationary sd >= 4 x cost. TP ~ the Bertram exit band (often 0.5-1 stationary sd), stop ~ 2.5-3.5 stationary sd. Refit every 30-60 min. If no (entry, exit) gives positive (m - a - c), stay idle for that session.

findings.mechanism: Stop-loss as ruin insurance whose cost you accept, with TP re-tuned to the stop (Kaminski-Lo, Leung-Li)
findings.description: Kaminski & Lo show that under a random walk a stop-loss always lowers expected return. Under momentum or regime-switching it can add value, in proportion to return persistence. Leung-Li show that with a stop, the optimal take-profit falls. So for a grid the basket stop is not an alpha source. It is insurance against the regime the grid cannot survive (persistent trends), and the TP must be re-optimised together with it. Mechanism for the EA: always run a hard basket stop sized by the risk budget, plus a broker-side SL on every ticket. Re-tune TP and spacing with the stop in place; don't take TP from a no-stop optimisation.
findings.blowup_protection: The stop makes the maximum loss per cycle deterministic (ignoring gaps). Since FX intraday shows continuation after large moves (see the depth finding), the stop earns a positive 'stopping premium' in exactly the tail that kills grids.
findings.hf_relevance: A per-position stop does not fit a grid that relies on averaging. A basket-level stop placed in sigma units beyond the last layer is the HF-compatible version. Combine it with the time exit so both price and time are bounded (triple-barrier style).
findings.evidence: Kaminski-Lo (search summary): under a random walk 'the stopping premium is always negative'; with momentum it 'can be positive and is directly proportional to the magnitude of return persistence'. Leung-Li: a higher stop-loss level implies a lower optimal take-profit. Lipton-LdP doc example: the optimal SR exit corridor is asymmetric (stop -3.41 vs profit +5.08 in scaled units), showing PT and SL must be co-optimised.
findings.parameter_hints: BasketStopMoney = RiskFraction x Equity (see Kelly). Place broker SLs so the aggregate loss at the stop price equals BasketStopMoney. After a stop: cooldown >= 30-60 min on that side and no size increase.

findings.mechanism: Session selection by measured reversion, liquidity and fix flows
findings.description: Institutional FX liquidity and volatility follow strong intraday patterns: a U-shape in EBS activity from 08 to 15 GMT, concentrated in the overlaps (Ito & Hashimoto). Rollover around 17:00 New York is a liquidity hole, and the 2016 sterling flash crash happened in thin early-Asian hours. Benchmark fixes create a W-shaped dollar pattern: the dollar appreciates before the Tokyo, Frankfurt and London fixes and reverses afterwards (Krohn-Mueller-Whelan, Evans). Mechanism for the EA: replace the hour filter with a per-session score from rolling data. Score = (VR30 < 0.9) AND (median spread <= 0.2 x TP) AND not within the pre-fix 30 minutes AND not within rollover +/- 45 min. Trade only the windows that pass.
findings.blowup_protection: It avoids the hours where large moves continue (London open, US data), where spreads blow out (rollover), and where liquidity is thin enough for flash events (early Asia on Mondays and holidays). All three are where grids take their outsized losses.
findings.hf_relevance: Own stats (inference, excluding news): VR30 by UTC hour is 0.74-0.85 at 00-04, 1.02-1.04 at 05-07 (London open, random-walk-like), 0.83-0.94 at 08-11, 0.92-0.96 at 12-13, 0.76-0.86 at 14-16, 0.78-0.85 at 17-19, 0.54-0.67 at 20-21. The 21-23 UTC hours revert most but are where spreads widen about 4x, so cost kills them. Best candidates: about 15:15-19:30 UTC (post-London-fix NY afternoon) and 00:30-04:30 UTC (Asia, lower sigma) on a tight-spread account.
findings.evidence: Krohn et al. JF 2024 (search summary): 'U.S. dollar systematically appreciates against all currencies ahead of the three major currency fixes in Tokyo, Frankfurt and London, while displaying a strong reversal pattern thereafter'. Evans (search summary): at month-end, 72% of the pre-fix-hour move is reversed by the next day's noon. BIS (search summary): GBP/USD fell 9.66% within 40 seconds in early Asian trading on 7 Oct 2016; time of day made the market more vulnerable. Baule et al. (search summary, equities): return reversals are most pronounced at 15-minute horizons and depend on how easily intermediaries can mean-revert inventories. Own VR table from hfstats.py (inference).
findings.parameter_hints: Initial allowed windows (UTC, re-validate per broker): 00:30-04:30 and 15:15-19:30. Blocked: 05:00-08:00, 12:00-14:30 (US data), the 30 min before the London 16:00 fix, 20:45-23:15 rollover, Monday before 01:00, Friday after 19:00. Last L1 at window_end - 30 min.

findings.mechanism: Directional drift skew by time of day (EUR weak in the European morning and pre-fix, strong after fixes / in US hours)
findings.description: Breedon & Ranaldo find currencies tend to depreciate during their own local trading hours. EUR/USD depreciates in the European morning and appreciates in US hours, and order flow shows the same pattern. Krohn et al. find the dollar appreciates into each major fix and gives it back afterwards. A symmetric two-sided grid ignores this predictable drift, so one side systematically fights it. Mechanism for the EA: add a small session drift term mu_session to the AS reservation price. In windows with known negative EUR drift (European morning, the 30-60 min before a fix), widen BUY spacing and tighten SELL TP. Do the reverse after fixes and in the US afternoon.
findings.blowup_protection: It reduces the chance that the side facing the drift fills to its cap. This is a second-order improvement; the caps and stops do the real protection.
findings.hf_relevance: The drift is small per 30-minute window and partly overlaps with the session filter. Use it as a skew coefficient only, never as a standalone signal, since the effect is small compared with spread costs (inference).
findings.evidence: Breedon-Ranaldo JMCB 2013 (search summary): 'EUR/USD tends to depreciate in the European morning and then appreciate in US trading hours'; the pattern is reflected in order flow. Cartea & Wang, Market Making with Alpha Signals (search summary): market makers use alpha signals to reduce adverse selection and to skew toward expected price moves.
findings.parameter_hints: mu_skew in [-0.2, +0.2] x sigma_15 shift of the reservation price. Fit the sign per window on in-sample data and keep it only if it survives walk-forward.

findings.mechanism: Scheduled-news blackout: flatten before, no adds during, slow restart after
findings.description: Andersen & Bollerslev find announcement effects on DM/USD volatility are large (the employment report raises volatility about 576%) and that the main impact is gone within 10-20 minutes, with elevated volatility for hours. Andersen-Bollerslev-Diebold-Vega find the conditional mean jumps almost immediately. Chaboud-Chernenko-Wright find the price jump comes before the volume surge, and that volume spikes even on in-line releases. Yamada & Ito find liquidity dries up before announcements and that liquidity recovery has become slower. Evans & Lyons find that at least half (about two-thirds) of the news effect reaches the price through subsequent order flow, i.e. persistent, informed, one-directional flow that a grid would absorb. Mechanism for the EA: block L1 from T-30 to T+60 (T+120 for NFP, FOMC, ECB and CPI). Force-close open baskets at T-5. No layer adds inside the window. After it, require sigma_15 back below 1.5 x seasonal before re-arming.
findings.blowup_protection: This removes the largest source of adverse-selection losses: adding layers into informed, one-directional post-news flow, with gaps that can jump the basket stop. Own stats (inference): inside [-30, +60] windows sd_1m = 5.0 pips vs 1.0-2.4 outside, VR30 = 1.05 (trending), and 30-minute one-sided MAE p99 = 99.6 pips vs 17.5-34.9 outside.
findings.hf_relevance: The user's backtest already found that the news filter plus pausing layers materially reduced drawdowns. At 1-30 minute holding, nearly every basket that overlaps a release is at risk, so pre-release flattening is cheap (baskets are short anyway).
findings.evidence: Andersen-Bollerslev 1998 (search summary): employment report volatility up 576%; 'the main impact seems to be gone within 10-20 minutes' with elevated volatility for several hours. Chaboud et al. (search summary): 'much of the immediate jump in prices in reaction to an announcement occurs before the surge in volume'. Yamada-Ito (search summary): 'Liquidity dries up prior to the announcement time'; the speed of liquidity recovery has slowed. Evans-Lyons (search summary): roughly two-thirds of the macro-news effect is transmitted via order flow.
findings.parameter_hints: Pre-block 30 min, close-all at T-5, post-block 60 min (120 for tier-1), layer adds frozen throughout. Re-arm only if spread <= 1.5 x median and sigma_15 <= 1.5 x seasonal. Use the MQL5 calendar (high impact, USD+EUR) live; the backtest calendar covers fewer events.

findings.mechanism: Unscheduled volatility-burst / jump circuit breaker (self-exciting jumps, toxic flow, market withdrawal)
findings.description: FX jumps are self-exciting. Hawkes studies of EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/CHF and USD/JPY at 15-minute frequency find significant self-excitation, with jump clusters lasting about 2.5-6 hours. Cartea-Jaimungal-Ricci model mutually exciting market orders: after a burst, the optimal market maker widens its postings by the expected jump size to defend against adverse selection. In the AS simulations, toxic fills mainly destroy the inventory P&L leg, and wider spreads help only when flow is toxic. hftbacktest's risk notes say to exit and wait when price behaviour or latency is abnormal. Mechanism for the EA: a circuit breaker on |1-min return| > 4 sigma_1m, or a 5-min range > 3 sigma_5, or spread > 2 x median, or tick gaps / ping spikes. It freezes adds and new L1 for 60-120 min, widens spacing x1.5 for the next 2-6 h, and lets open baskets exit only via TP (shrunk), the time exit or the stop.
findings.blowup_protection: It catches the unscheduled shocks the news calendar misses (central bank headlines, flash events) and stops the grid feeding inventory into a jump cluster. Jump clusters are when gaps through stops and broker stop-outs happen.
findings.hf_relevance: Very high. These events unfold within minutes, exactly the grid's holding horizon, and the clustering means the next 2-6 hours are riskier than average.
findings.evidence: Jump-clustering study (search summary): 'strong evidence of statistically significant self-exciting behavior in time series of large jumps'; clusters last 2.5-6 hours on average. CJR (search summary): market orders can induce midprice jumps, so agents increase their postings by the expected jump size. iqueipopg (fetched): with 30% toxic fills, the symmetric strategy's inventory P&L fell to -20.7 while spread capture stayed 68.0; the inventory-skewed strategy's was -12.1. Seb-L-P (fetched): at xi=0.20 adverse selection, AS 56.43 vs naive 53.77, Sharpe 9.04 vs 3.26. hftbacktest (fetched): 'it is advisable to withdraw from the market in such situations'.
findings.parameter_hints: Burst = |r_1m| > 4 sigma_1m(seasonal) OR range_5m > 3 sigma_5 OR spread > 2 x 20-day same-hour median. Freeze 60-120 min. Spacing multiplier 1.5 for 4 h after a burst. Log every trigger for review.

findings.mechanism: Regime gate: trade only when the short-horizon process is mean-reverting (variance ratio / change-point / regime probability)
findings.description: A grid is a short-volatility, short-gamma position. Quantpedia note it is the reverse of delta-hedging, so it profits when price oscillates and loses when it trends. Stat-arb practice gates trades by regime: the Markov regime-switching arbitrage rule only takes reversion entries when the regime probability P(s_t) >= rho, to avoid trading through structural breaks. The Taranto-based MQL5 grid EA uses CUSUM change-point detection plus regime-aware gating, so cycles run only in favourable regimes. Mechanism for the EA: on each M5 bar compute VR(15) or VR(30) over the last 2-4 hours, a trend t-stat (60-min drift / sigma), and a CUSUM of signed returns. Arm L1 only if VR < 0.9 and |t| < 2 and no CUSUM alarm. A CUSUM alarm mid-basket freezes adds on the side facing the move.
findings.blowup_protection: Persistent trends are the only thing that ruins a capped grid quickly, through repeated full-depth stops. The regime gate cuts how often the grid is armed into them.
findings.hf_relevance: VR and CUSUM are cheap enough to compute in MQL5 on M1 data. Our data shows VR varying from 0.54 to 1.05 by hour and news state (inference), so the gate will be selective.
findings.evidence: Quantpedia (search summary): 'grid trading is basically reverse to delta hedging' (short volatility). Regime-switching doc (fetched): enter long only if X_t <= mu_1 - delta*sigma_1 AND P(s_t=1|X_t) >= rho; the purpose is to avoid structural breaks where 'temporary spread deviations ... become persistent'. MQL5 article (search summary): unconstrained grids face almost-sure ruin; the remedy is 'finite, restartable cycles with regime-aware gating', ATR spacing, CUSUM and a kill switch.
findings.parameter_hints: VR window 120-240 M1 bars, threshold 0.9. Trend gate |sum r_60|/(sigma_1m sqrt(60)) < 2. CUSUM k = 0.5 sigma, h = 4-5 sigma. Re-arm after an alarm only after 30-60 min of quiet.

findings.mechanism: Fractional Kelly on the lower confidence bound of the basket win rate (negative-skew sizing)
findings.description: A grid basket pays off like a short option: frequent small wins, rare large losses. For a binary bet with win prob p, payoff ratio b = W/L and q = 1-p, f* = (p*b - q)/b. For negatively skewed bets f* is extremely sensitive to p (inference math). Example: W=1, L=9 gives f* = 20% at p=0.92, 10% at p=0.91, 0 at p=0.90. Pinning p to +/-1pp at 95% needs about 3,000 baskets. Thorp: the probability that wealth ever falls to a fraction x of its start is x^(2/c - 1) at c times Kelly (x at full Kelly, x^3 at half Kelly). Betting about 2x Kelly drives growth to zero, and overestimating the edge is the usual way to overbet. Practitioners use 25-50% Kelly, smaller when skew and estimation error are high. Mechanism for the EA: RiskFraction per basket = min(0.25 x f*(p_LCB, b), 1-2% of equity). p_LCB is the 95% lower bound of the live/forward-test win rate; W and L come from realised basket P&L net of cost.
findings.blowup_protection: Sizing on the lower bound of an uncertain, skewed edge stops the classic grid failure: a high in-sample win rate leads to aggressive size, and one tail event wipes out months. With no proven edge (p_LCB below breakeven), Kelly says the size should be the minimum, i.e. paper or demo trading only.
findings.hf_relevance: HF grids produce many baskets per week, so p can be estimated faster than for swing systems. Re-estimate monthly; the tails still need years of data.
findings.evidence: Thorp (search summary): P(V_t/V_0 <= x for some t) = x^(2/c - 1); c=1 gives x, c=1/2 gives x^3. MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba (search summary): in a real-data example half Kelly had max drawdown 25% vs 48.4% at full Kelly and 94.3% at triple Kelly. Half Kelly gives about 75% of the growth at about 50% of the volatility. Betting 2 x f* gives negative growth (search summary). Option-trading Kelly note (search summary): the 2-moment Kelly approximation breaks down for skewed payoffs. Atlas Peak (search summary; lower-quality source): negative skew significantly reduces the Kelly fraction. Own example (inference): f*(0.92) = 0.20, f*(0.91) = 0.10, f*(0.90) = 0; n = 4p(1-p)/0.01^2 = about 2,944 baskets for +/-1pp.
findings.parameter_hints: Use p_LCB = p_hat - 1.96 sqrt(p_hat(1-p_hat)/n). If f*(p_LCB) <= 0, trade the minimum lot on demo only. Cap RiskFraction at 1-2% of equity per basket. Use realised basket win/loss distributions including stops and time exits, not the TP/SL design values.

findings.mechanism: Drawdown floor (Grossman-Zhou / CPPI) exposure scaling plus a layered kill switch (FIA practice)
findings.description: Grossman & Zhou show that to keep wealth above a fraction alpha of its running peak, the optimal risky exposure is proportional to the cushion W_t - alpha*M_t. Exposure goes to zero at the floor, so the floor is never breached in continuous trading. FIA's automated-trading guidance makes pre-trade limits (max order size, max position) and a kill switch standard. The kill switch disables new orders and cancels working orders but allows risk-reducing orders. Mechanism for the EA: RiskMoney per basket = m x (Equity - alpha x PeakEquity). Add a daily loss limit, a weekly limit, and a hard kill at the floor that flattens everything and requires a manual restart. Put broker-side SLs on every ticket so protection survives a disconnect.
findings.blowup_protection: This turns 'don't blow the account' into an explicit, mechanically enforced floor. After losses, position size shrinks automatically (anti-martingale), the opposite of recovery-martingale behaviour.
findings.hf_relevance: HF grids can fire many cycles per session, so a fast daily stop matters. Pre-trade checks (spread, max lots, margin level after the order) should run on every add, not just on L1.
findings.evidence: Grossman-Zhou (search summary): with constraint W_t >= alpha*M_t, the optimal policy invests in risky assets 'in proportion to the surplus W_t - alpha*M_t' (CPPI with a floor at a multiple of the running max). FIA (search summary): pre-trade max order size and position limits; a kill switch 'immediately disables all trading activity ... cancelling all working orders' and 'may also allow for risk-reducing orders'.
findings.parameter_hints: alpha = 0.75 (25% max DD from peak), m chosen so that at peak the risk per basket is 1-2% of equity. Daily loss limit 3-4% of start-of-day equity: halt until the next day. Weekly limit 8%. Hard kill at the floor: flatten, disable the EA, manual review. Pre-trade margin check: projected margin level after the add >= 300% (well above the broker's 50% stop-out).

findings.mechanism: Finite, restartable cycles with no recovery martingale, monitored by floating-vs-closed drawdown (DDR)
findings.description: Taranto & Khan model grid trading as a bi-directional grid-constrained stochastic process with absorbing barriers at ruin and at a profit target. Grids reach ruin more slowly than a gambler's-ruin bettor, which makes them look profitable short-term, but unconstrained operation is still ruinous. Zarattini & Aziz show that martingale sizing on random signals can produce an apparently 20%-per-year system with nearly 80% probability, a short-term illusion. The 2026 HF-grid paper defines DDR = max equity DD / max balance DD and reports 5.72 (80% floating vs 14% closed). Mechanism for the EA: every basket is a finite cycle (TP, time exit or stop) followed by a cooldown. Lots never increase after a loss. The EA reports and alerts on equity-based drawdown and DDR, never balance alone.
findings.blowup_protection: This removes the 'win back the loss' feedback loop that turns a bad day into ruin. Monitoring floating drawdown exposes hidden risk that a balance-only equity curve masks until the blow-up.
findings.hf_relevance: With hundreds of short cycles a month, a balance curve looks smooth even while floating risk spikes. DDR and max floating loss per cycle are the right live KPIs.
findings.evidence: Taranto-Khan (search summary): grid trading 'whilst still subject to the risk of ruin' generates higher short-term returns, and the grid problem takes longer to reach ruin than gambler's ruin. Zarattini-Aziz (search summary): martingale on random signals 'can seemingly generate a 20% annual return with nearly 80% probability'. MDPI (search summary): DDR 5.72, equity DD 79.97% vs balance DD 13.98%. Martingale (search summary): with finite bankroll or limits, the optional stopping theorem rules out long-run profit.
findings.parameter_hints: Cooldown after a stop: 60 min on that side, and after 2 stops in a day stop the session. Alert when DDR > 2 or when max floating loss > 2 x RiskMoney. Never let BaseLot depend on the last basket's result.

findings.mechanism: Round-number and stop-cluster awareness for TP and layer placement (Osler)
findings.description: Osler's data on real currency stop-loss and take-profit orders shows take-profits cluster at round numbers, while stops cluster just beyond them. Trends therefore tend to reverse at round numbers and accelerate once they are crossed (stop cascades). Mechanism for the EA: (1) if a computed TP lies within 1-2 pips beyond a 00/50 level, pull it inside the level; (2) don't add a new layer in the 3-5 pips just past a round number that price has just crossed in the adverse direction, where cascades run; place the basket stop beyond the likely stop cluster, not just inside it.
findings.blowup_protection: It avoids adding inventory right where cascades accelerate, a micro-version of 'don't average into momentum'.
findings.hf_relevance: Relevant at a pip scale that matters for 3-8 pip grids. Small effect; treat as a refinement.
findings.evidence: Osler (search summary): 'trends tend to reverse course at predictable support and resistance levels, and trends tend to be unusually rapid after rates cross such levels'; take-profits cluster at round numbers, stops just beyond.
findings.parameter_hints: Round levels: every 50 pips (x.xx00, x.xx50). TP snap distance 1-2 pips. No-add zone: 0-5 pips beyond a freshly crossed round level, for 15 min.

findings.mechanism: Trade partially toward the target inventory instead of in fixed jumps (Garleanu-Pedersen)
findings.description: With trading costs and a mean-reverting signal, the optimal policy is to 'aim in front of the target' and 'trade partially toward the current aim'. The target is a cost-free optimal position, here Jurek-Yang's linear-in-deviation inventory. For a grid this means each layer adds only part of the gap between current and target inventory. The target is capped by Q and decays with the basket clock. Mechanism for the EA: inventory target q* = clamp(-k*(P - EMA)/sigma^2 * Equity, -Q, +Q), multiplied by (1 - t/T_max). Add a layer only when q* - q exceeds one lot step. Reduce when q exceeds q*, e.g. by partial closes as the time limit approaches.
findings.blowup_protection: Inventory follows a bounded, time-decaying target instead of growing mechanically with distance. Combined with the cap, the EA can't build exposure that the model would not want even with costs.
findings.hf_relevance: It formalises the time-decaying TP and the no-adds-after-T_add rule into one inventory rule that fits MQL5 (one target per bar).
findings.evidence: Garleanu-Pedersen (search summary): the optimal strategy is characterised by two principles: '1) aim in front of the target and 2) trade partially towards the current aim'; signals with slower alpha decay get more weight. Jurek-Yang (fetched): the target allocation is linear in the mispricing and proportional to wealth.
findings.parameter_hints: Trade rate 0.3-0.5 of the gap per M1 bar. Target multiplied by (1 - t/T_max). Hard clamp to +/-Q. This is an alternative to fixed spacing; test it as a variant, not as a replacement on day one.

failure_modes.mode: Convex lot ladder with no hard stop in a persistent trend
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: With +LotIncrement or doubling, loss grows quadratically or exponentially with distance, while the expected gain per cycle stays fixed. One significant trend (2014-15) erases all prior cycles. Ladder math on $100 (inference): 6 layers +0.01/layer at 10-pip spacing lose $56 at one spacing past the last layer; the v6.12 18-layer ladder is about $78/pip once full. Persistence beyond about 3 sigma is the norm, not the exception, in London/NY at 15-30 minutes.

failure_modes.mode: Paying the spread for an edge smaller than the spread
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: Institutional grid and market-making profits come from earning the spread or rebates. Bank dealers' 30-minute speculation was not profitable. A retail grid pays about 1.2+ pips round trip per layer, while the measured average reversal after 1-3 sigma moves is about 0.2-0.5 pips (own data, inference). Net expectancy is negative, so the account slowly bleeds, and the operator then 'fixes' it with bigger size or more layers, which brings on the tail failure.

failure_modes.mode: Holding or adding through scheduled news and unscheduled jumps
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: Releases produce immediate price jumps (before the volume surge), multi-hour volatility, thin pre-release liquidity and informed one-way order flow. Jumps cluster for 2.5-6 hours. Stops get gapped and a grid keeps buying into informed flow. Own data (inference): 30-minute one-sided MAE p99 is about 100 pips in news windows vs 17-35 pips outside.

failure_modes.mode: Trading thin-liquidity hours: rollover, early Asia, holidays
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: Spreads widen several-fold around the 17:00 New York rollover, which wipes out small TPs and triggers spread-induced stops. Flash events (GBP -9.66% in 40 s in early Asia, Oct 2016) happen when liquidity is thinnest and blow through any ladder before the EA can react.

failure_modes.mode: Time stop without a price stop (or the reverse)
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: A 30-minute cap alone does not cap loss: 99.9th-percentile one-sided moves within 30 minutes are about 55-60 pips in London/NY and about 150 pips around news (own data, inference). A price stop alone lets baskets sit for hours or days and pay swap (the largest cost in the user's study). Both barriers are needed.

failure_modes.mode: Over-sizing from an over-estimated win rate (negative skew plus Kelly sensitivity)
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: For payoff ratio W/L = 1/9, a 1-percentage-point error in win rate halves the Kelly fraction and a 2pp error makes it zero (inference). Betting more than about 2x Kelly drives growth to zero or below. Grid backtests show high win rates that are not statistically separable from breakeven without thousands of baskets.

failure_modes.mode: Martingale-shaped equity illusion and overfitting
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: Averaging down makes even random signals look profitable most of the time (about 80% chance of a 20%/yr-looking system). The balance curve hides floating risk (DDR 5.72 in a 2026 HF-grid study). Optimisers then select the configurations whose tail event simply did not occur in-sample, consistent with the user's failed walk-forward (WFE -0.61 to -0.68).

failure_modes.mode: Recovery behaviour after losses (raising size or removing limits to win back)
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: Under a finite bankroll the optional-stopping argument rules out a positive long-run result for doubling schemes. Raising size after drawdown is the reverse of the Grossman-Zhou/CPPI rule (exposure proportional to cushion above the floor) and converts a recoverable drawdown into ruin.

failure_modes.mode: Ignoring net inventory and predictable intraday drift with two symmetric grids
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: With both grids open, one side is always fighting the move. Without inventory skew, inventory follows a random walk (final-q std about 3x that of the AS-skewed strategy). Predictable session and fix drifts (EUR weak in the European morning and into fixes) push the same side to its cap repeatedly.

failure_modes.mode: Minimum-lot granularity on a $100 standard account
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: At 0.01 lot = $0.10/pip (0.1% of equity per pip), even a single layer stopped at about 14-17 pips costs 1.4-1.7%, and 3 flat layers at 1-sigma spacing cost 2.7-3.4% (inference). There is no room for proper fractional sizing or 'scale up per layer' without exceeding a sane per-basket risk. Ladders that look small in lots are large relative to equity, and broker stop-out at 50% margin level arrives fast.

failure_modes.mode: No infrastructure risk controls (disconnect, latency, abnormal spreads)
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: If the EA's stops are virtual and the terminal disconnects, or quotes become abnormal, nothing limits the loss. Professional practice is pre-trade limits, a kill switch and withdrawing from the market when latency or prices are abnormal. Grids without broker-side SLs rely on the terminal being up during the worst minutes.

failure_modes.mode: Base rates for leveraged retail FX
failure_modes.why_accounts_blow: Regulators report that 74-89% of retail CFD accounts lose money. Any design whose expectancy depends on many small wins against rare large losses should be assumed losing until a live forward test with realistic costs shows otherwise.

(1) Short-horizon mean reversion is real but tiny:

BOTTOM LINE for the orchestrator:
- The institutional evidence says market makers survive through hard inventory caps, inventory skew, short inventory half-lives, flattening before the horizon, pulling out around news and jumps, and drawdown-floor sizing. All of these translate into concrete EA mechanisms (findings above).
- Their profits come from earning the spread, which a retail MT5 grid pays instead. So these mechanisms can make the 1-30 minute grid survivable (bounded loss per cycle, no blow-up), but the literature and our data do not support positive expectancy unless costs are very low (raw-spread ECN or a tight cent account), trading is limited to the measured mean-reverting windows, and a forward test shows the win rate's lower confidence bound above breakeven.
- The user's wish to 'scale up per layer' conflicts with Jurek-Yang (linear, wealth-scaled inventory, reduced beyond a critical deviation) and with the Kelly/Thorp results. Recommend flat lots per layer, sized by equity and sigma.
- On a $100 standard account, the 0.01 minimum lot leaves only about 2-3 flat layers within a 2-3% per-basket risk. A cent account is needed for real sizing granularity.

Suggested EA parameter set to backtest first: M5 trigger; sessions 00:30-04:30 and 15:15-19:30 UTC; spacing 1.0 x sigma15; TP 0.6 x sigma15 from the average, decaying to break-even plus cost between 10 and 30 minutes; MaxLayers 3, flat lots; no adds after 15-20 minutes; hard 30-minute close; basket stop at 3 x sigma15 from L1 with broker-side SLs; news blackout from 30 minutes before to 60-120 minutes after, with close-all 5 minutes before; burst breaker; daily -4%, weekly -8%, kill at -25% from peak. The project's backtester (research/bgrid_bt.py) already has max-hold, session-close and daily-stop parameters for testing this.

findings.mechanism: Finite, restartable grid cycles with an unconditional age limit (Taranto BGC model)
findings.description: Each cycle picks an anchor price, builds the grid, trades under supervision, and closes on whichever comes first: profit target, drawdown threshold, age limit, or the weekend rule. It then restarts at current prices, which resets both accumulated variance and grid exposure to zero. The age exit fires regardless of P/L. The article bases this on Taranto's PhD result that an unconstrained grid leads to almost-sure ruin, while finite cycles with regime gating can have positive expected value under the right conditions.
findings.blowup_protection: Caps how long a basket can sit in the market, so the adverse excursion it can meet stays bounded (the variance of a random walk grows with time). It removes the open-ended 'wait for the market to come back' holding that caused every $100 no-stop config to blow up in our backtests.
findings.evidence: Code Base defaults (from snippets): InpRuinThreshold 0.25 (25% equity kill), InpProfitTargetPercent 3.0, InpMaxCycleHours 72. The kill switch is checked every tick and measures the drop from equity at cycle start. Snippet: if a single cycle runs indefinitely the trader eventually loses; ending and restarting the cycle resets the time variable to zero.
findings.hf_relevance: The user's 30-minute hard maximum is the high-frequency version of this. Apply it to the WHOLE grid, using the age of the oldest open layer, not only to each position. After an age exit, restart from a new anchor only if all gates pass again. Inference: going from a 72h to a 0.5h cycle shrinks the 1-sigma excursion by about sqrt(144) = 12x, so ladder depth can and should be much shallower than v6.12's 18 layers.
findings.parameter_hints: Hard grid age 30 min (user requirement). Inference: add a soft age at about 10-15 min after which the TP collapses toward breakeven plus costs. Measure the kill switch from equity at cycle start and size it for $100 (about 2-3%), not the 25% default, which assumes large accounts and 72h cycles.

findings.mechanism: Regime gating: volatility/drift ratio gate plus a CUSUM change-point detector, which pick the grid mode
findings.description: BGC Grid EA has three modes chosen at each cycle restart. BGT (bi-directional, buy and sell at each level) is for ranging markets where volatility dominates drift. TGT (stop orders in the trend direction only, no per-trade TP, basket exit) is used when the sigma/mu ratio or a CUSUM break signals a trend. MGT (counter-trend limit orders with TP toward the anchor) runs after a failed TGT cycle to catch post-trend reversion. VolatilityGate computes sigma_t/mu_t (ATR vs drift magnitude) on a regime timeframe (default H4), with cooldown-based state changes. CPDEngine runs a frozen-baseline CUSUM to catch abrupt breaks the ratio filter would see too slowly.
findings.blowup_protection: Stops the symmetric two-sided grid from running when drift dominates, which is exactly when one side piles up layers. The CUSUM break catches sudden regime shifts (data releases, liquidity events) faster than a smoothed filter. MGT gets a tighter kill threshold because it carries more structural risk.
findings.evidence: From article/code/forum snippets. No public backtest numbers came through in the snippets.
findings.hf_relevance: The user's EA always opens BUY and SELL grids together, i.e. permanently in BGT mode. For an M1/M5 scalper, compute the gate on M15-H1 over the last few hours (inference) and open the symmetric pair only when sigma/mu is high, meaning ATR is large relative to net drift. After a CUSUM break, block new cycles for a cooldown period.
findings.parameter_hints: Default regime TF H4 (source). For a 30-min holding horizon, inference: sigma = ATR(M5, ~24), mu = |close - close[n]| / n or EMA slope over the same window; require sigma/mu above a calibrated quantile; block for N bars after a CUSUM alarm.

findings.mechanism: Live exposure in grid-level units; floating loss grows quadratically with depth; margin stop-out arrives before the 'last level'
findings.description: The Taranto article measures drawdown in grid levels, D_t = floor((SessionHigh - Price)/g), and states that after n levels of one-way movement the cumulative loss is the triangular number n(n+1)/2 steps (quadratic growth). GridCapitalCalculator makes the same point: a chain of N legs floats at step x N(N-1)/2, so 10 legs is 45 steps of loss, not 10. Open legs also lock margin while they float, and stop-out is a percentage (for example 50%), so the account dies while the chain 'still looks recoverable'. The tool computes the adverse move that ends the account, then counts how often a move that large has already happened in the symbol's own M1 history.
findings.blowup_protection: Gives the EA (and the trader) the real worst-case before each add, instead of the misleading 'loss at the last level' figure, and ties that worst case to an empirical frequency on M1 data.
findings.evidence: Formulas from both sources. GridCapitalCalculator reports: 'Adverse move that ends it', 'Times in the last N days', and 'A full chain is: floating plus margin as % of equity'.
findings.hf_relevance: Inference, arithmetic applied to the user's EA on $100 (0.01 lot = $0.10/pip). Flat 0.01 ladder with spacing s pips and N layers: loss at the last fill = $0.10 x s x N(N-1)/2, and each further pip costs $0.10 x N. Example: s=4, N=4 gives $2.40, then $0.40/pip. With the user's +0.01-per-layer ladder (0.01, 0.02, ...), the loss at the last fill is $0.10 x s x (N^3 - N)/6: N=6, s=3 gives $10.50 (10.5% of equity) before any stop slippage. The v6.12 live set (0.08 base, 18 layers, 8 lots max) cannot fit a $100 account at all. Recommended use: run the GridCapitalCalculator-style 'how often did a move this large happen within 30 minutes, by hour of day' on the Oanda M1 data to pick spacing and depth.
findings.parameter_hints: Budget per grid side, inference: worst-case (all layers filled + basket stop) <= 2-2.5% equity. That implies about 3 flat 0.01 layers at 3-4 pip spacing on $100.

findings.mechanism: Pre-trade basket simulation with auto-fit of layer count, plus hard volume limits
findings.description: RecoveryPilot simulates every basket to its last level before the cycle starts. If the planned loss exceeds a set percentage of balance, the cycle is rejected; with auto-fit on, the level count is reduced until the plan fits (keeping at least one recovery level). It also has hard limits on max levels, max lot per position, max total lots and broker volume limits, plus margin checks, a basket stop (percent of balance at cycle start, or a fixed amount) and broker-side SL/TP.
findings.blowup_protection: Worst-case loss is decided and bounded BEFORE the first order. The grid can never be configured, or drift into, a depth the account cannot carry.
findings.evidence: User-guide snippet listing: pre-trade simulation, auto-fit, hard limits, margin checks, limit action, basket stop, equity brake, lock time, broker-side SL/TP.
findings.hf_relevance: Directly fixes the 'ladder depth x spacing is the binding constraint' problem on $100. Before every new BUY/SELL grid, compute the worst case from current ATR-based spacing, current spread and the planned lot ladder. Trim MaxLayers so it is <= the risk budget, or skip the cycle.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: reject threshold about 2-2.5% equity per grid side and about 4% for both sides combined; auto-fit minimum 2 layers; per-position max lot 0.02; total open lots cap about 0.06-0.08 on $100 standard.

findings.mechanism: Equity brake from the high-water mark, lock time after a stop, and a daily loss limit
findings.description: RecoveryPilot's equity brake closes the basket if equity falls X% below its high and locks trading until the user presses START. Its lock time blocks new cycles for X minutes after a basket stop or limit action. Grid Scalper MA's daily drawdown (% of start-of-day balance, default 10%) closes losers, trails winners and opens no new baskets until the next day. Prop-firm style monitors compute daily limit = account x daily %, and max-loss floor = account x (1 - max %).
findings.blowup_protection: Breaks the chain of trend days where each new cycle re-enters the same move. Turns an open-ended loss sequence into a bounded daily loss.
findings.evidence: Snippets from RecoveryPilot guide, Grid Scalper MA product page and Prop Firm Daily Loss Tracker code page.
findings.hf_relevance: Critical at M1 frequency. After a basket or time stop during a burst, an immediate new cycle usually sits inside the same impulse. A 30-120 min lock (inference) after a losing stop plus a daily stop sharply cuts the 'death by many cuts' path our news-filter tests partly addressed.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference for $100: daily loss stop 4-5% of start-of-day balance; equity brake 6-8% below the equity high-water mark, needing manual restart; lock 60 min after any loss exit larger than 1% equity.

findings.mechanism: Hard basket stop loss with a small, fixed level count, defined in percent
findings.description: Osloma Gold allows at most 4 grid levels and applies a predefined hard stop to every basket. Its Model A ($150 basket SL) has a higher win rate but slower recovery; Model B ($100 SL) wins slightly less often but recovers faster. Burning Grid removes martingale entirely, gives every strategy a predefined exit at a controlled loss (for example 1% risk per Buy strategy), and strictly limits open positions per symbol. Basket Protective Close recommends percent-of-balance/equity limits over fixed money because a fixed amount changes meaning as the account changes. At trigger it snapshots the basket tickets, retries failed closes on a 0.5 s timer, picks the right filling mode, verifies server return codes, and waits instead of giving up while disconnected or the market is closed.
findings.blowup_protection: Turns the tail from 'margin call on the broker's terms' into a planned loss of known size. Robust close logic keeps the stop working during fast M1 moves and requotes.
findings.evidence: Osloma blog (max 4 levels, $100/$150 models); Burning Grid blog/product (1% per strategy example, kill switch); Basket Protective Close code page (snapshot, retry, filling mode).
findings.hf_relevance: The user's EA has only an 'optional basket stop on float loss % of reference capital'. For the HF $100 version it should be mandatory, per grid side, in % of equity, and combined with the 30-min age exit. Use the snapshot+retry close pattern because 1-30 min scalps hit fast markets.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: per-side basket stop = min(2-2.5% equity, one spacing beyond the deepest layer). Max levels 3-4 (the Osloma choice of 4 is a useful anchor).

findings.mechanism: Honest measurement: a hard-capped grid still loses without a gross edge
findings.description: A developer built three XAUUSD grids and measured them. System 1 was a volatility-sized recovery grid with a hard equity stop on the whole sequence. The cap held across about 1,000 sequences with zero violations, yet the system lost $2,456 over four years, and only $128 of that was costs. System 2 had a 98.5% win rate over 844 trades but finished -23.2%: one sequence on 16 Apr 2025 lost $4,425, while the second-worst loss in thirteen years was $132. System 3 (someone else's realistic grid) won 92.3% of trades and still ended -86.2%. Key line: a grid converts a small probability of a very large loss into a high probability of a small gain; cap the large loss and you remove what was paying for the small gains.
findings.blowup_protection: Not a protection mechanism but an acceptance criterion. Stops and caps bound ruin; they do not create edge. The design has to find positive gross expectancy elsewhere.
findings.evidence: Quantitative results quoted above (blog snippet).
findings.hf_relevance: Matches our own finding that the unfiltered symmetric grid has about zero gross edge and is negative after spread and swap. For the HF version, the edge has to come from (a) choosing sessions/regimes where M1 returns are measurably anti-persistent, (b) lower cost per round trip, (c) inventory skew and exit timing. It will not come from the lot ladder. Inference: run the backtest with the full stack of stops FIRST, and accept the design only if the stopped version is still net positive out of sample.
findings.parameter_hints: Acceptance tests (inference): positive net expectancy with stops on, in walk-forward and in a 2014-15 trend-stress window; worst cycle loss <= the pre-trade budget.

findings.mechanism: 'Smart grid' cooldown: stop adding layers when market structure turns against the basket
findings.description: Grid Scalper Pro tracks trend from its own swing sequence. When a basket's direction is confirmed against the prevailing trend, that basket enters cooldown and stops adding levels entirely. It is not closed; it simply 'refuses to keep feeding a move it has no evidence is finished'. It resumes adding only after a change of character (CHoCH) confirms a structural reversal. The same EA treats spacing as a curve and stores basket state in SQLite so a restart does not orphan a live basket.
findings.blowup_protection: Stops the quadratic depth growth during trends. Combined with a time exit, a basket in cooldown is closed at shallow depth instead of being averaged deeper.
findings.evidence: Blog and product snippets describing cooldown and CHoCH resume.
findings.hf_relevance: The user already pauses layer adds during news; extend this to structure. Inference: on M1 execution, read swings on M5/M15; if the basket side is against a confirmed M5/M15 swing trend, stop adding. The 30-min age exit then closes it small. Persisting state across restarts matters for a VPS-run scalper (the user's EA already recomputes from live positions, which is good).
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: swing detection on M5 with a 3-5 bar fractal; resume only after a CHoCH or after the cycle is closed by age.

findings.mechanism: Choice of action at the max-trades cap ('Hold' vs 'Close all'), VWAP-breakeven-plus-buffer TP, trailing on the first trade only
findings.description: Grid Scalper MA caps trades per basket and lets the user choose the action at the cap: 'Hold' (stop adding, wait for recovery) or 'Close all' (close the basket as soon as the cap is hit). It also caps simultaneous baskets (default 3). Baskets close at the volume-weighted breakeven plus a 'Breakeven Points' buffer (default 50 points), recalculated as layers are added. Trailing applies only to the first trade of a basket, after a minimum profit. Daily drawdown % (default 10%) blocks new baskets until the next day.
findings.blowup_protection: 'Close all at cap' turns MaxLayers into a hard depth stop instead of the start of an unbounded hold. A single-trade trail lets lone winners run without adding risk.
findings.evidence: Product page snippets with defaults.
findings.hf_relevance: The user's EA already has a live VWAP +/- TP_Pips TP that is recomputed after every add; that part matches this design. Add: (1) Close-all at MaxLayers for the $100 version; (2) single-position trailing while the grid has one fill; (3) a TP buffer that shrinks with depth and age. Inference: Poljakov's grid math indicates that as N grows the needed distance approaches half the profit, so deep baskets should target breakeven plus costs, not the full TP.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: TP_buffer = max(4 x round-trip cost, k x ATR(M5)) for 1-2 layers; breakeven plus 1 x cost for 3+ layers or age > 10-15 min.

findings.mechanism: Rolling grid that cuts exposure: close the OLDEST layer when price runs off range instead of adding
findings.description: PZ Grid Trading EA's default 'Regular' behavior for an off-range grid is to cut exposure. It closes the oldest trade (the one with the open price furthest from current price), takes a partial loss, and lets the grid range move one spacing with the market. The alternative 'Averaging' behavior instead tries to exit at the average price of all trades.
findings.blowup_protection: Open inventory never exceeds N layers; losses are realized in installments rather than as one catastrophic stop, and the basket follows a trend instead of fighting it with more size.
findings.evidence: User-guide snippet.
findings.hf_relevance: A good fit for 1-30 min holding. The oldest layer is also the one that will hit the 30-min age limit first. Inference: implement a 'sliding window' of at most N flat 0.01 layers; when price passes one spacing beyond layer N, close layer 1 and open a new layer at market. Each slide costs about N x s pips x 0.01 lot (realized), and inventory stays constant. Must be backtested against the plain basket stop, because each slide realizes a loss.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: N=3, s from the ATR rule; limit to 2-3 slides per cycle before the basket stop applies.

findings.mechanism: Partial-close recovery: pair the furthest losing layer with winners (compensatory trailing / close-by-profitables / first-last overlap)
findings.description: AB Universal Grid's Compensatory Trailing Stop (CTS) groups the losing position furthest from price with all profitable ones and computes a breakeven only for that group, which is much closer to price than the overall breakeven. It trails a real server-side SL for that group and keeps adding further losers whenever they can be covered. Priority 1 is to compensate as many losers as possible; priority 2 is to trail profit. AW Close By Profitables finds the most unprofitable position, searches for a set of profitable positions whose profit covers it, closes them together, and caps how many profitable orders may be used. Grid EA Pro, AW Smart Grids ('Use_overlap_last_and_first_orders'), Trend Line GRID and Grid MT4 Recovery switch on a 'drawdown reduction' overlap after a set number of orders, closing the most distant losers against counter-profit.
findings.blowup_protection: Shrinks the deepest, most expensive layer early, which reduces the quadratic tail and the margin locked. Server-side SLs keep protection working through disconnects.
findings.evidence: Blog/product snippets (mechanism descriptions; no quantitative results in the snippets).
findings.hf_relevance: The user's EA is a hedging account with two magic-isolated grids. Inference: within a grid, when (oldest loser + newest winner(s)) has P/L >= cost buffer, close them as a group, which cuts depth without waiting for the full VWAP TP. Cross-grid compensation (using the SELL grid's realized TP profit within the same cycle to retire the BUY grid's oldest loser) is possible but breaks the 'SetTP never touches the other grid' isolation, so keep it as a separate, explicit module. Caveat: overlaps realize losses; with zero gross edge they only reshape the distribution.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: activate at >= 3 layers; require group net >= +0.5 pip x group lots after costs; max 2 winners per loser.

findings.mechanism: Volatility-scaled spacing with a cost floor and expansion per level
findings.description: Community EAs size spacing as Step = ATR x coefficient, recalculated before each new order. Grid Scalper Pro treats spacing as a curve (static, contraction, expansion or hybrid, scaled by a % per level). Zone-recovery manuals say a per-level zone expansion of 1.1-1.5 'noticeably reduces whipsaw risk at the cost of a wider worst case', and the zone should be at least 20-25 spreads (the panel turns amber below 20x). A gold basket EA uses distance = max(min points, ATR x multiplier) x density. BGC recomputes spacing from daily ATR at each cycle restart. Gold 1 Minute Grid offers ATR presets (Adventurous = small/high-frequency, Balance, Safe = larger spacing).
findings.blowup_protection: Wider spacing in fast markets means fewer layers fill per pip of adverse move. Expansion makes the depth in pips grow faster than the layer count, so the quadratic loss term grows more slowly. A spread-multiple floor stops costs from eating every TP.
findings.evidence: Snippets; the 20-25x spread rule and the 1.1-1.5 expansion range are explicit.
findings.hf_relevance: The user's 7.5-pip fixed spacing came from M15 tuning. For 1-30 min holds, inference: s1 = max(3 pips, k x ATR(M5,12), 3 x round-trip cost) with expansion of about 1.25 per level. Example: 3.0 / 3.75 / 4.7 pips puts layer 3 at 6.75 pips; with flat 0.01 x 3 the loss at L3 is about $1.05 and a stop one gap further is about $2.2 total on $100. The 20x-spread rule cannot be met on a standard account at 30-min horizons (1.3 pip x 20 = 26 pips), which is a strong hint that only raw-spread accounts make an HF grid viable.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: k about 0.8-1.5 x ATR(M5); expansion 1.2-1.5; floor 3 x (spread + commission in pips); recompute at each new cycle and freeze within the cycle so VWAP math stays stable.

findings.mechanism: Flatten the lot ladder: same-size second layer, adaptive multiplier, and 'bigger fixed lot beats martingale'
findings.description: A survival-oriented martingale design opens the second recovery order at the SAME lot as the first, increases size only gradually, and automatically lowers the multiplier once open orders pass a threshold. It hard-caps orders per cycle around a pre-calculated worst case and has a portfolio kill switch. A 55-strategy study found that, at equal profit, a plain bigger fixed lot gave less drawdown and about one-third to one-half the risk of ruin of martingale. Example: martingale 1.3 (cap 8) had DD 21 and RoR 3.6% vs fixed 1.5x with DD 20 and RoR 1.6%; martingale 2.0 had DD 35 and RoR 11.0% vs fixed 2x with DD 26 and RoR 4.0%. Doubling from 0.01 reaches 1.28 lots after seven losers, while fixed-lot recovery keeps margin linear. Modified Grid-Hedge Part IV shows a multiplier of 2 puts breakeven 2D/3 below the first order.
findings.blowup_protection: Size is not concentrated exactly where losses are already stacking. Margin and floating loss grow roughly linearly per layer (quadratic over depth) instead of exponentially.
findings.evidence: Quantitative comparison from the 55-strategy blog; 0.01 to 1.28 lots example; 2D/3 breakeven math.
findings.hf_relevance: The user asks to 'start 0.01 and scale up per layer'. On $100 standard, the evidence and the depth arithmetic both favor flat 0.01 for the first 2-3 layers and at most one step to 0.02. The current +LotIncrement ladder is arithmetic, so the loss at depth grows with (N^3-N)/6 (inference). If more size is wanted, grow BaseLot with equity (a 'bigger fixed lot'), not lots per layer.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: ladder 0.01, 0.01, 0.01 (optionally 0.02 on layer 4 only if the pre-trade sim passes); MaxTotalLots per side 0.04; BaseLot = 0.01 per $100-150 equity, re-evaluated daily.

findings.mechanism: Inventory-aware two-sided quoting (Avellaneda-Stoikov reservation price and volatility-scaled spread)
findings.description: An MQL5 article implements Avellaneda-Stoikov. The fair (reservation) price shifts against current inventory to push the book back to flat, and the quoted spread widens with volatility and narrows with liquidity. It notes a fixed grid placing buy and sell limits at a constant distance 'has no memory of how much inventory it is holding and no sense of how volatile the market has become'. Over 5,000 EURUSD H1 bars, the AS maker kept inventory near zero: std 0.411 vs 1.405 lots (-70.8%), final inventory 0.30 vs 4+ lots, P&L 710.52 vs negative for the fixed-spread maker. The author warns this is a single run, not a forward edge.
findings.blowup_protection: Limits how much one-sided inventory can build up, which is the market maker's main risk and the same thing as one grid side running deep.
findings.evidence: Table values from the article snippet; caveat from the author.
findings.hf_relevance: This is the institutional framing of the user's dual-grid design: the BUY grid and SELL grid are two quotes, and net inventory q = buy lots - sell lots. Inference adaptation: when q > 0 (long-heavy), widen the next BUY layer's spacing and/or stop BUY adds, and tighten the SELL grid's entry/TP so fills re-flatten; mirror for q < 0. Scale both spacings with short-horizon sigma. This is a per-tick rule that fits the 1-30 min horizon better than a fixed ladder.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: block adds on the heavy side when |q| >= 0.02-0.03 lots on $100; skew spacing by a factor (1 + gamma x |q|/0.01) with gamma about 0.25-0.5; derive sigma from M1 returns over the last 30-60 min.

findings.mechanism: Session selection: trade the quiet Asian-session range and avoid the rollover hour
findings.description: The MQL5 article on night trading says EURUSD volatility usually falls and price moves flat during the Asian session (unlike the JPY crosses). Its system trades 1:00-11:00 MSK, using Bollinger Bands to detect the flat channel; the two tests returned 152% and 48% with drawdown under 25%. Night-scalper guidance: do not open during the rollover hour when spreads widen and liquidity is thin; use a max spread of about 10 points and preferably a 2-5 point broker. Grid EAs commonly apply time filters only to NEW baskets while grid management, trailing and daily-DD protection keep running outside hours. Night Hunter Pro reviews warn that the edge decayed (consistently negative since 2022-2023 per one reviewer), that slippage in night trading is a big issue, and that one bad trade can wipe out one or two months of gains.
findings.blowup_protection: Concentrates exposure in the hours when EURUSD's short-horizon behavior is closest to mean-reverting, and keeps out of the spread spikes that turn small-TP scalps negative.
findings.evidence: Article results (152% / 48%, DD < 25%); night scalper setup notes; product reviews.
findings.hf_relevance: The user's hour filter already gates new grids only, which matches this practice. Inference: let the data choose the window. For each hour of day in the 2012-2020 M1 set, measure lag-1 autocorrelation of 1-min returns, the 30-min max adverse excursion, and the spread distribution. Trade only hours with significantly negative autocorrelation and low excursion, and exclude rollover +/- 30-60 min (server-time and DST aware). Expect edge decay: revalidate yearly.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference starting window: roughly 23:30-06:00 UTC excluding the rollover window; max spread <= 1.5 x that hour's median spread; no new cycle in the last 30 min before rollover so the 30-min cap also prevents swap.

findings.mechanism: Graded news handling: block initial trade, block all trades, or close before release; one-cancels-other news engine
findings.description: Waka Waka's news filter has escalating actions: prohibit the initial trade, prohibit all trades, or close all trades before the release. Grid EA news panels set pause-before/after windows (a 120-minute default in one FAQ), let impact levels be filtered, and let events be reclassified to high impact by keyword (FOMC, CPI, Nonfarm). A gold basket EA design has a separate OCO news branch that suspends normal entries for the whole day when a qualifying high-impact USD event is scheduled.
findings.blowup_protection: Removes jump risk that a diffusion-based grid cannot price, and prevents adds into post-news momentum.
findings.evidence: Product/blog snippets.
findings.hf_relevance: Our backtests already showed the news filter + layer-add pause materially reduced drawdowns. For 1-30 min holds, 'close all before news' is cheap because positions are young. Inference: no new cycle 30-60 min before, flat 5 min before, resume 30-60 min after; treat FOMC/NFP/ECB days as session-wide blocks.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: Tier-1 (FOMC, NFP, CPI, ECB) block -60/+60 min and force flat at T-5 min; Tier-2 block -30/+30 min without force-close.

findings.mechanism: Account-level basket risk aggregation: VWAP, swap-inclusive P/L, margin, count, and 'time underwater'
findings.description: An MQL5 risk-management series aggregates the EA's own positions into a basket. It computes volume-weighted entry, floating P/L including swap, and used margin, then enforces limits on combined loss, margin, position count and time underwater. It warns that two or three individually valid stacked/averaged/hedged trades can quietly turn 1% per trade into 3-6% total exposure. Part 6 extends this to portfolio and correlated risk at account level.
findings.blowup_protection: Prevents the illusion that each layer or each grid is 'within risk' while the total is not. The time-underwater limit is a structural stop.
findings.evidence: Article snippets.
findings.hf_relevance: The user isolates grids by magic number for TP, which is correct for TP. Risk limits (combined float loss, total lots, margin) should be evaluated on the union of both grids. 'Time underwater' equals the 30-min cap. Include swap and commission in the P/L used by every limit.
findings.parameter_hints: Inference: combined float-loss stop about 4% equity across both grids; total lots across both <= 0.08 on $100.

findings.mechanism: Risk-of-ruin fingerprinting and payoff-asymmetry tests as acceptance gates
findings.description: The Hidden Risk of Ruin Auditor reads closed-trade history and scores four fingerprints: volume escalation after a loss (martingale), overlapping same-direction exposure at worse prices (grid/averaging), payoff asymmetry (many small wins vs a disproportionate loss), and classical risk of ruin at a stated risk per trade. These combine into an A-F grade. A companion blog gives the arithmetic: 95% wins x $2 vs 5% losses x $45 = -$0.35 expectancy.
